scenes.narration: [punch] **Five hundred thousand** dollars a year.
For a rookie who had never played a single NBA game.
[tense] About **three times** the best shoe deal around.
From a company that had just lost money.
For a player who didn't even want their shoes.
[excited] Today, that bet brings in more than **five billion dollars** a year.

visual.label: JORDAN BRAND REVENUE, PER YEAR (MORE THAN)

scenes.narration: [curious] Stick around. You'll see why it was less crazy than it looks.
And why the people involved still disagree about who made the call.
[calm] Summer, nineteen eighty-four.
Nike has hit its first real bump.
For ten years, the company grew like a weed.
Under thirty million dollars in sales in nineteen seventy-three.
**Eight hundred sixty-seven million** by the end of eighty-three.
[tense] Back in February, the streak broke.
Nike posted its first quarterly loss. **Ever.**
It's been a public company since nineteen eighty, so every quarter gets judged.
And a rival called Reebok is coming up fast.
In basketball, Nike's playbook is coaches.
Since nineteen seventy-seven, a marketer named Sonny Vaccaro has signed about **eighty** college coaches.
Their teams play in Nike.
[curious] Now meet the player. **Michael Jordan.**
College player of the year.
The Chicago Bulls take him third in the NBA draft, on June nineteenth.
Two players went before him.
[build] He wore Converse in college.
He wanted Adidas.
And Nike?
[punch] He had never even worn a **pair**.
So here's what Nike knows. He's the best college player in the country.
He has never played a pro minute.
And his heart is set on **Adidas**.
[calm] At Nike, the names to know: Phil Knight, co-founder and boss. Rob Strasser, the marketing chief. And Vaccaro.
For Jordan, his agent: **David Falk**.
[tense] Remember those names. The credit fight lasts for decades.
[build] Here's where it gets interesting. Nike is about to smash the record. **By a lot.**
[tense] So sit in Nike's chair.
First, the case for walking away.
You just lost money.
A rival is gaining on you.
The kid hasn't played a single pro game.
Nobody knows if he can carry an NBA team.
[build] He doesn't want your shoes. He wants **Adidas**.
If he flops, you've paid a record price for a bench player. And everyone **sees it**.
And the competition? Converse is offering him about **a hundred thousand** dollars a year.
[build] Now look at Nike's number.
Five hundred thousand a year. For five years.
[punch] About **two and a half million** dollars in cash.
Roughly three times the best shoe deal in the game.
Remember that number.
Add stock options, and by Falk's count the package could reach about **seven million**.
[curious] And here's a twist most retellings skip.
Nike's offer wasn't even the biggest in cash.
According to ESPN's reporting, a brand called Spot-Bilt bid **more**.
So money alone wasn't going to win this.
[curious] Now flip it around. Here's the case for signing.
Nike can't beat Converse by copying Converse.
So it offers something different.
His own **shoe line**. His name on it.
And royalties: a cut of the sales.
Plus, by Falk's account, a million dollars of marketing in the first six months.
[calm] And the risk is smaller than it looks.

visual.text:
THE RISK IS
SMALLER THAN IT LOOKS.

scenes.narration: Nike's yearly sales were about eight hundred sixty-seven million dollars.
Jordan's fee was **less than a tenth of one percent** of that.

visual.title: JORDAN'S FEE VS NIKE'S YEARLY SALES

scenes.narration: Even in its rough year, Nike still made over forty million in profit.
If this failed, Nike would survive.
[build] Then there's the exit. According to Falk, the contract had an escape hatch.
The targets: Rookie of the Year. An All-Star team. Twenty points a game.
[punch] Miss them in his first three years, and Nike could walk away **two years early**.
A record bet, with a capped downside.
[curious] But first, Nike had to get him on a plane.
Jordan didn't want to go.
His parents talked him into it.
[build] At Nike's headquarters in Oregon, they played him a highlight tape.
The soundtrack: the Pointer Sisters' "Jump."
They pitched a shoe built around him.
And by Falk's telling, Strasser even pulled out two toy **Mercedes** cars.
[tense] So here's the table.
A company that just lost money.
A rookie who wants someone else.
A price three times the record.
And a rival with more cash.
[curious] You're Nike. Would you **sign** him? Take a second. Really sit with it. Comment SIGN or PASS before I tell you.
[pause 0.8] [calm] Jordan gave Adidas one last chance.
"I was very loyal," Jordan said, as quoted by ESPN.

visual.speaker: Michael Jordan, as quoted by ESPN, 2013

scenes.narration: He took Nike's offer back to Adidas and said: "This is the Nike contract, if you come anywhere close, I'll sign with you guys."

visual.text: This is the Nike contract, if you come anywhere close, I'll sign with you guys.
visual.speaker: Michael Jordan, as quoted by ESPN, 2013

scenes.narration: [tense] Here's the strange part. According to ESPN's reporting, Adidas had shown almost no interest.
And Adidas didn't come close.
[build] Nike had the shoe. The royalties. The plan.
[punch] That fall, Michael Jordan **signed** with Nike.
[excited] Five hundred thousand a year.
His own shoe. A cut of every pair.
[warm] Remember the kid who'd never worn a pair?
In his own words: "In all honesty, I never wore Nike shoes until I signed with Nike."

visual.text: In all honesty, I never wore Nike shoes until I signed with Nike.
visual.speaker: Michael Jordan, USA Today, 2015

scenes.narration: [tense] But signing him was the **easy part**.
The NBA banned his red and black Nike shoes.
The reported fine: **five thousand dollars** a game.
[build] Nike could have backed down.
Instead, by most accounts, it paid.
[excited] Then it turned the ban into an ad.
Its punchline: "Fortunately, the NBA can't keep you from wearing them."

visual.text: Fortunately, the NBA can't keep you from wearing them.
visual.speaker: Nike's "banned" ad, as quoted by ESPN

scenes.narration: [build] Then came the shoe.
The Air Jordan One hit stores in the spring of nineteen eighty-five.
Sixty-five dollars a pair.
Nike's goal? Three million dollars in sales. Over three **years**.
[build] By May, they'd sold...
[excited] **Seventy million** dollars' worth.
By the end of the first year? [punch] More than **a hundred million**.
More than thirty times the goal, in a third of the time.
[calm] And that escape hatch? Never needed.
Jordan was Rookie of the Year.
He made the All-Star team.
[curious] Most people stop the story here.
But the biggest numbers came later.
And not in a **straight line**.
[tense] By the mid-eighties, Reebok had passed Nike as America's biggest athletic shoe maker.
By nineteen eighty-eight, Reebok had lost that top spot.
[build] In nineteen ninety-seven, Jordan became a brand of its own.
It kept growing. And growing.
Year one: more than a hundred million.
Remember the contract? About two and a half million dollars.
[excited] In twenty twenty-two alone, Jordan Brand brought in **five point one billion**.
[punch] That's about **two thousand times** the whole cash deal. In a single year.
[curious] And Jordan himself? Reported Nike earnings that year: one hundred fifty to two hundred fifty-six million dollars.
That cut of the sales made him a **partner**, not just a face.
[excited] And Nike as a whole? From eight hundred sixty-seven million in sales... to **forty-six point four billion**.
That's fiscal twenty twenty-six. About fifty times bigger.
[calm] Not all of that is Jordan. But he's the bet everyone remembers.
Jordan later put it this way: "Would the brand have been as strong if it was adidas? We'll never know."

visual.text: Would the brand have been as strong if it was adidas? We'll never know.
visual.speaker: Michael Jordan, ESPN, 2013

scenes.narration: [curious] So who actually made the call?
Back to that fight. Vaccaro says he picked Jordan and urged Nike to spend its whole allotted budget on him.
Knight and Jordan dispute his role.
[build] The twenty twenty-three movie goes further: Vaccaro bets his job, and the whole basketball division, on one **rookie**.
For that version, we found no source beyond Vaccaro's own account.
[calm] Phil Knight credits Strasser and designer Peter Moore.
About Vaccaro, Knight said: "Sonny helped, but he wasn't the MVP in that process."

visual.text: Sonny helped, but he wasn't the MVP in that process.
visual.speaker: Phil Knight, USA Today, 2015

scenes.narration: Jordan credits Strasser and coach George Raveling.
[somber] Vaccaro was fired by Nike in nineteen ninety-one.
Knight summed up the whole fight in one line: "Success has a thousand fathers and failure is an **orphan**."

visual.text: Success has a thousand fathers and failure is an orphan.
visual.speaker: Phil Knight, USA Today, 2015

scenes.narration: [build] A losing quarter. A rookie with zero NBA games. Three times the best deal around.
[punch] **Signed.**
[warm] When you're behind, copying the leader is the real risk. Bet big on what only you can offer, but write yourself an exit.

visual.text: Bet big on what only you can offer. Write yourself an exit.

metadata.description:
In 1984, Nike had just posted its first quarterly loss ever. Reebok was closing in. And Nike was about to offer $500,000 a year, about three times the best shoe deal around, to a rookie who had never played an NBA game and who wanted Adidas.

Today that bet brings in more than five billion dollars a year. But it was less crazy than it looks, and the people involved still disagree about who made the call. Sit in Nike's chair, then find out what happened.

Would you have signed? Tell us in the comments.
